summary: Tractate Yoma opens with the Mishnah's rule that seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is separated from his home to the Chamber of Parhedrin, and another kohen is prepared in case he becomes disqualified; Rabbi Yehuda wants another wife prepared too, lest his wife die, since 'his house' in the verse means his wife, but the Sages answer that if so there is no end to the matter. The Gemara cites the parallel Mishnah in Parah: the kohen who burns the parah adumah is likewise separated seven days beforehand, to the Chamber of the Stone House facing the Bira to the northeast, so called because all its service used dung, stone, and earth vessels. The reason for those vessels is that a tevul yom is fit for the parah (the kohen was even deliberately made tamei and immersed, to refute the Sadducees who required sunset), so the Sages required vessels that cannot become impure, so that people would not treat the parah lightly. The chamber is in the northeast as a distinguishing sign: the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting. Rabbi Yochanan explains 'Bira' as a specific place on the Temple Mount, and Reish Lakish as the whole Temple. Finally, Rabbi Yochanan derives both separations from the inauguration verse 'as the Lord commanded to do, to atone for you': 'to do' is the parah and 'to atone' is Yom Kippur. When the Gemara asks why the whole verse should not refer to Yom Kippur, it answers with a verbal analogy on 'tzivah' linking the verse to the parah statute. The daf ends as the Gemara begins a further challenge ('ve'eima'), which continues on the next daf.

display.title: Mishnah: The Kohen Gadol separates seven days before Yom Kippur
display.oneLine: The KG is sequestered in the Parhedrin chamber with a backup priest; Rabbi Yehuda wants a backup wife too, but the Sages say that leads to infinite regress.
display.shortSummary: The Mishnah establishes the KG's mandatory seven-day retreat to the Parhedrin chamber before Yom Kippur, with a backup priest designated in case of disqualification. Rabbi Yehuda extends this logic to require a backup wife, since the service requires the KG to be married. The Sages reject this on infinite-regress grounds.
display.whats: The Mishnah opens Yoma with the Kohen Gadol's mandatory week-long retreat to the Parhedrin chamber before Yom Kippur. He needs a backup priest in case he becomes tamei or otherwise disqualified. Rabbi Yehuda goes further: designate a backup wife too, since the Yom Kippur service requires the Kohen Gadol to be married ('and for his house' means 'his wife'). The Sages reject this - if you start planning for every contingency, there is no stopping point.
display.hint: If the Mishnah prepares a backup Kohen Gadol, why do the Sages refuse to prepare a backup wife?

learning.learnerQuestion: If the Sages prepare a backup Kohen Gadol, why not prepare for every possible failure - including the death of his wife?
learning.coreTension: Rabbi Yehuda applies the same preparatory logic consistently; the Sages counter that consistency here leads to an infinite chain of contingency-planning that cannot terminate.
learning.coreMove: The Sages invoke 'ein la'davar sof' - infinite regress - as a formal rejection of an otherwise coherent extension of the rule.
learning.resolution: The Sages object to the backup-wife proposal on the grounds that, if accepted, there would be no end to the matter.

takeaway.text: Halachic preparation for contingencies is bounded by the practical ability to terminate the chain. A rule that generates infinite new obligations cannot stand.

reasoningPattern.notes: Classic Talmudic rejection pattern: 'ein la'davar sof' terminates rules that cannot self-limit.

learning.ahaMoment: The Sages' retort 'if so, there is no end to the matter' implies that any rule requiring a backup for every contingency has no natural limit.
learning.learningBlocker: The source records the Sages' objection to Rabbi Yehuda tersely: if that concern is valid, there is no end to the matter, since the replacement wife could also die.
learning.memoryAnchor: The Sages respond to Rabbi Yehuda's backup-wife proposal only by objecting that it would create a chain with no end.

argumentFlow.label: Opening rule
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: Seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is separated from his house to the Chamber of Parhedrin, and another kohen is prepared in his place in case a disqualification befalls him.

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Yehuda extends the logic
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbi Yehuda
argumentFlow.text: Also designate a backup wife, since 'his house' in Leviticus 16:6 means his wife - and if she dies, he cannot perform the service.

argumentFlow.label: Infinite regress
argumentFlow.speaker: Chachamim
argumentFlow.text: If so, that this is a concern, there is no end to the matter - what if the designated replacement wife herself dies?

sourceRefs.note: The Sages' objection: ein la'davar sof

misconceptions.misconception: The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda because they deny that 'his house' in the verse means his wife.
misconceptions.correction: The Sages do not dispute that derashah in the Mishnah. Their only stated objection is that if one prepares for the wife's death, there is no end to the matter.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the Mishnah require a backup priest to be designated in advance?
quizSeeds.answer: In case the KG becomes tamei or suffers another disqualifying event before Yom Kippur, so the service is not interrupted.

quizSeeds.question: What is Rabbi Yehuda's proof that the KG must be married to perform the Yom Kippur service?
quizSeeds.answer: Leviticus 16:6 says 'and he shall atone for him and for his house' - 'his house' is interpreted as his wife.

quizSeeds.question: Why do the Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's proposal to designate a backup wife?
quizSeeds.answer: It creates infinite regress - the backup wife could also die, requiring another backup, with no stopping point.

sugyot.finalRuling: A backup priest is designated; a backup wife is not.
alternateAngles: The Sages' retort 'if so, there is no end to the matter' rejects Rabbi Yehuda's proposal because it would lead to an endless regress of contingencies.
prerequisiteKnowledge: The Kohen Gadol must be married to perform the Yom Kippur service (Leviticus 16:6 - 'and for his house').

display.title: Gemara: The parah adumah parallel and the Stone House chamber
display.oneLine: Before sourcing the KG's seven-day rule, the Gemara notes that the parah adumah priest was also sequestered for seven days in the northeast Stone House, using only dung, stone, and earth vessels.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara opens by drawing a parallel to the red heifer priest, who was also separated for seven days and housed in the northeast Stone House chamber. The chamber's name comes from the requirement to use only stone, dung, and earth vessels in its service.
display.whats: Before asking where the seven-day rule comes from, the Gemara notes that the parah adumah priest was also separated from his home for seven days and housed in the northeast Stone House chamber. The chamber got its name from the requirement to use only stone, dung, and earth vessels in its service. This parallel isn't coincidental; it is the key to the Gemara's later derivation.
display.hint: Why does the Gemara introduce the parah adumah case right here, before sourcing the law for the Kohen Gadol?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Gemara open the tractate by jumping to the parah adumah before even asking where the KG's seven-day rule comes from?
learning.coreTension: The parah adumah case looks like a detour, but the Gemara needs it on the table because its seven-day separation parallels the Kohen Gadol's, which is the subject of the mishna.
learning.coreMove: Juxtapose the two cases before sourcing either, so the reader sees their structural identity and is primed for the derivation.
learning.resolution: The parah case is not a digression: the Gemara cites the Mishnah in Parah, which also separates the kohen who burns the parah from his house for seven days, as a parallel to the Kohen Gadol's separation in this Mishnah.

takeaway.text: When the Gemara introduces a parallel case early, it usually returns to link them formally. The parallel is the argument.

reasoningPattern.notes: The parah adumah is introduced as a structural twin to the KG case, priming the gezerah shavah derivation.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara's opening move is to establish that two laws share the same feature (seven-day separation) before proving they share the same source.
learning.learningBlocker: The parah adumah seems like a tangent; it is actually the argument in embryo.
learning.memoryAnchor: The parah kohen's seven-day separation (Lishkat Beit HaEven, northeast) parallels the Kohen Gadol's seven-day separation before Yom Kippur - the Gemara puts both cases on the table as parallel halakhot.

argumentFlow.label: Parallel case introduced
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Just as the Kohen Gadol is removed from his house for seven days, the priest who burns the parah adumah was also removed from his house for seven days to the chamber that was before the bira, in the northeast, which was called the Stone House.

argumentFlow.label: Why 'Stone House'?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The chamber was called the Stone House because all the actions associated with the heifer were performed using dung, stone, and earth vessels - vessels that cannot become ritually impure.

misconceptions.misconception: The parah adumah case is a digression before the main topic.
misconceptions.correction: It is the structural setup presenting the parallel mishna about the parah kohen's separation alongside the Kohen Gadol's.

visualizableElements.item: The Chamber of the Stone House, facing the Bira to the northeast

quizSeeds.question: Where did the parah adumah's Stone House chamber get its name from?
quizSeeds.answer: From the requirement to use only dung, stone, and earth vessels in its service.

quizSeeds.question: What second seven-day separation rule does the Gemara cite from the Mishnah in Parah, and how does it parallel the Kohen Gadol's separation?
quizSeeds.answer: The kohen who burns the parah adumah is also separated seven days beforehand, to a chamber called Lishkat Beit HaEven, facing the Bira to the northeast.

sugyot.finalRuling: The kohen who burns the parah adumah is separated from his house seven days beforehand to the chamber facing the Bira to the northeast, the Chamber of the Stone House.

display.title: Why dung, stone, and earth vessels? Balancing the tvul yom leniency
display.oneLine: Because a tvul yom is fit to burn the parah, as shown by the practice of deliberately making the kohen tamei and immersing him to refute the Sadducees, the Sages required vessels that cannot become tamei, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara explains why the parah's service used only dung, stone, and earth vessels. A tvul yom is fit to perform the parah, as the Mishnah in Parah shows: the kohen was deliberately made tamei and immersed, to refute the Sadducees, who held that it could be done only by one whose sun had set. Because of that leniency, the Sages instituted vessels that cannot receive impurity, so that people would not come to treat the parah lightly.
display.whats: Why were all the parah's acts done with dung, stone, and earth vessels? Because a tvul yom, one who immersed today and whose sun has not yet set, is fit to perform the parah. The Mishnah in Parah proves it: they would deliberately make the kohen who burns the parah tamei and immerse him, to refute the Sadducees, who said it was done only by those whose sun had set. Since the parah is lenient in this respect, the Sages instituted vessels that cannot receive impurity at all, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.
display.hint: If a tvul yom is fit to burn the parah, why did the Sages respond by requiring vessels that cannot become impure at all?

learning.learnerQuestion: If a tvul yom is fit to perform the parah, why did the Sages insist that its vessels be made only of materials that cannot become impure?
learning.coreTension: The halacha is lenient in allowing a tvul yom to perform the parah, a leniency even demonstrated publicly against the Sadducees; yet a lenient purity standard risks people treating the parah's purity lightly.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara explains a rabbinic stringency, vessels that cannot become impure, as a counterweight to a leniency, that a tvul yom is fit for the parah, citing the Mishnah about deliberately immersing the kohen as proof of that leniency.
learning.resolution: Because a tvul yom is fit for the parah, the Sages instituted dung, stone, and earth vessels that cannot receive impurity, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.

takeaway.text: Where the halacha permits a leniency in a sensitive rite, the Sages may add a compensating stringency so that the leniency does not lead people to treat the rite lightly.

reasoningPattern.notes: A rabbinic safeguard is justified as a counterweight to a halachic leniency: since a tvul yom is fit, vessels that cannot become impure keep people from disregarding the parah's purity.

learning.ahaMoment: The dung, stone, and earth vessels do not show that the parah is stricter by nature; the Gemara explains them as a response to its leniency, since a tvul yom is fit to perform it.
learning.learningBlocker: Students often stop at 'stone vessels cannot become tamei' without asking why that mattered here specifically.
learning.memoryAnchor: Tvul yom is fit for the parah (the kohen was even made tamei and immersed to refute the Sadducees, who required sunset), so the Sages required vessels that cannot become impure, lest people treat the parah lightly.

argumentFlow.label: Why so stringent?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: What is the reason all the parah's acts were done with dung, stone, and earth vessels?

argumentFlow.label: Tvul yom is valid; Sages prove it publicly
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Because a tvul yom is fit to perform the parah. Proof: the Mishnah teaches that they would make the kohen who burns the parah tamei and immerse him, to refute the Sadducees, who said it was performed only by those whose sun had set.

argumentFlow.label: Secondary safeguard: impurity-proof vessels
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Therefore the Sages instituted dung, stone, and earth vessels, which do not receive impurity, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.

misconceptions.misconception: The vessels that cannot become impure were instituted to refute the Sadducees.
misconceptions.correction: The deliberate immersion of the kohen refuted the Sadducees. The vessels were instituted because a tvul yom is fit for the parah, so that people would not treat it lightly.

visualizableElements.item: The kohen, made tamei and then immersed that day (a tvul yom), burning the parah
Dung, stone, and earth vessels, which cannot receive impurity

quizSeeds.question: Why did they deliberately render the parah adumah priest impure?
quizSeeds.answer: To publicly demonstrate against the Sadducean rule that required sunset (haarev shemesh) before performing the heifer ritual, showing that a tvul yom is in fact valid.

quizSeeds.question: Why did the Sages require dung, stone, and earth vessels for the parah?
quizSeeds.answer: Because a tvul yom is fit for the parah, the Sages required vessels that cannot receive impurity, so that people would not treat the parah lightly.

sugyot.finalRuling: A tvul yom is fit to perform the parah adumah, and the Sages required that its service use dung, stone, and earth vessels, which cannot receive impurity.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Tvul yom: a person who immersed today but sunset hasn't arrived yet.
Sadducean position: the parah adumah could be performed only by a kohen whose sun had set after immersion, not by a tvul yom.

display.title: Why was the chamber placed in the northeast?
display.oneLine: The Stone House chamber was in the northeast: the parah adumah is classified as a chatat (associated with the north) and the ceremony faces the Tent of Meeting entrance (east) - northeast marks both, serving as a distinguishing indicator.
display.shortSummary: The Sages chose the northeast corner of the Temple courtyard for the parah adumah chamber because the parah is classified as a chatat, associated with the altar's north side, and the ceremony must be performed facing the Tent of Meeting entrance, which faces east. The corner functions as a heikher, a distinguishing marker combining both associations.
display.whats: Why northeast? The parah adumah is classified as a chatat, which is associated with the north side of the altar, and its ceremony must be performed 'before the opening of the Tent of Meeting,' which faces east. The Sages placed the sequestration chamber at the corner that evokes both associations, so the location itself serves as a heikher, a distinguishing marker of the ritual's classification.
display.hint: The chamber's location is a 'distinctive indicator' - of what exactly, and why does that matter?

learning.learnerQuestion: What is different about the northeast corner that led the Sages to house the priest performing the red heifer ritual specifically there?
learning.coreTension: The parah's chatat status points north and its verse 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' points east, yet neither requires its chamber to be in any place; the Sages chose the northeast to give it a distinguishing sign.
learning.coreMove: The Sages placed the chamber at the northeast so that its location carries a recognizable sign (heikher) of two scriptural features of the parah: it is a chatat (north) and its verse faces the Tent of Meeting (east).
learning.resolution: Northeast corner = north (the parah's chatat classification) + east (facing the Tent of Meeting). The location is a symbolic heikher, not a literal fulfillment of either requirement on its own.

takeaway.text: Physical placement can encode halakhic requirements, making the location itself a heikher (distinctive indicator) that keeps the law vivid for those performing it.

reasoningPattern.notes: Two scriptural features of the parah, its chatat status (north) and facing the Tent of Meeting (east), are signaled together by one rabbinically chosen location, not literally fulfilled by it.

learning.ahaMoment: The chamber is not just housing - it is a mnemonic device. Its location teaches the priest the law before the ritual even begins.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may not realize the parah adumah is classified as a chatat, which is the key to the north requirement.
learning.memoryAnchor: Northeast chamber: north for the parah's chatat status, east for facing the Tent of Meeting; a distinguishing sign (heikher) instituted by the Sages.

argumentFlow.label: Why northeast?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: What is distinctive about the northeast corner that led the Sages to place the parah chamber there?

argumentFlow.label: Chatat = north; faces east
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Because the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and of the parah it is written 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' (Numbers 19:4), which points east, the Sages instituted a chamber to the northeast.

argumentFlow.label: Location as distinctive indicator
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Sages placed the chamber in the northeast so the location itself serves as a heikher - a built-in orientation cue to keep the priest alert to both requirements.

misconceptions.misconception: The northeast location is arbitrary Temple geography.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara explains the northeast as a rabbinic choice: the parah is a chatat, a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting; the location serves as a distinguishing sign (heikher), not as the fulfillment of a directional requirement.

visualizableElements.item: Temple Mount compass diagram: north (chatat), east (Tent of Meeting entrance), northeast (sequestration chamber)

quizSeeds.question: Why is the red heifer ritual linked to the north side, leading the Sages to locate its chamber in the northeast?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the parah is classified as a chatat (sin-offering), and chatat offerings require the slaughter and sprinkling of blood to be performed north of the altar.

quizSeeds.question: What does 'heikher' mean in the context of the northeast chamber used for the red heifer ritual?
quizSeeds.answer: A distinctive indicator (heikher) - the northeast location made the priest vigilant in performing the ritual properly.

sugyot.finalRuling: The Sages instituted that the parah kohen's chamber be to the northeast as a distinguishing sign, since the parah is a chatat, and a chatat requires the north, and its verse speaks of facing the Tent of Meeting.
prerequisiteKnowledge: A chatat offering's slaughter must be performed on the north side of the altar.
The Tent of Meeting entrance faces east.

display.title: What does 'bira' mean? Rabbi Yohanan vs. Reish Lakish
display.oneLine: Rabbi Yohanan says 'bira' was a specific named spot on the Temple Mount; Reish Lakish says it means the entire Temple complex, citing David's prayer in Chronicles.
display.shortSummary: A brief lexical debate about the word 'bira' from the Para mishna. Rabbi Yohanan holds it was a specific named location on the Temple Mount. Reish Lakish holds it means the whole Temple, citing David's description of the future Temple as 'the bira I have prepared.'
display.whats: The Gemara pauses to clarify the word 'bira.' Rabbi Yohanan: it was a specific location on the Temple Mount with that name. Reish Lakish: 'bira' means the entire Temple compound, citing David's prayer in Chronicles where he calls the future Temple 'the bira I have prepared.'
display.hint: This looks like a minor geography dispute. Is 'bira' a landmark's proper name, or a general term for the whole Temple?

learning.learnerQuestion: Is 'bira' a specific spot on the Temple Mount, or a term for the whole Temple?
learning.coreTension: Rabbi Yohanan treats 'bira' as a proper noun (a named place); Reish Lakish treats it as a common noun applied to the whole Temple.
learning.coreMove: Verse-based definition: Reish Lakish derives the broader meaning from David's use of 'bira' in Chronicles for the entire future Temple.
learning.resolution: The dispute is left unresolved here; both views are preserved.

takeaway.text: Hebrew words in Mishnaic geography can be proper names (specific locations) or common nouns (categories). Reading them correctly requires knowing which function the word serves in each context.

reasoningPattern.notes: Classic dispute between specific toponym vs. generic category in Mishnaic geography.

learning.ahaMoment: Reish Lakish's proof from Chronicles shows that 'bira' was also used as a term for the entire Temple complex, as opposed to Rabbi Yochanan's view that it refers to a specific place on the Temple Mount.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume both Amoraim are defining the same kind of thing; Rabbi Yochanan names one specific place on the Temple Mount, while Reish Lakish applies the word to the entire Mikdash.
learning.memoryAnchor: Rabbi Yohanan: bira is a specific place on the Temple Mount. Reish Lakish: bira is the whole Temple, per David's 'the bira I have prepared' in Chronicles. The dispute is whether the word names a landmark or a category.

argumentFlow.label: What is 'bira'?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: What is the meaning of the term 'bira'?

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Yohanan: specific named place
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbi Yohanan (via Rabba bar bar Chana)
argumentFlow.text: There was a specific place on the Temple Mount called 'bira'.

argumentFlow.label: Reish Lakish: the whole Temple
argumentFlow.speaker: Reish Lakish
argumentFlow.text: The entire Temple is called 'bira', as David uses it in Chronicles: 'the bira I have prepared.'

misconceptions.misconception: Both Amoraim agree that 'bira' refers to the whole Temple and differ only about the proof verse.
misconceptions.correction: Rabbi Yochanan, quoted by Rabba bar bar Chana, says Bira was a specific place on the Temple Mount; Reish Lakish says the whole Mikdash is called Bira, citing 'the Bira which I prepared'.

visualizableElements.item: Temple Mount schematic with 'bira' labeled as either a spot or the whole complex

quizSeeds.question: What are the two opinions about what 'bira' means in the Para mishna?
quizSeeds.answer: Rabbi Yohanan: a specific named place on the Temple Mount. Reish Lakish: the entire Temple compound (as in David's phrase 'the bira I have prepared' in Chronicles).

quizSeeds.question: What is Reish Lakish's proof that 'bira' means the whole Temple compound?
quizSeeds.answer: He cites I Chronicles 29:19, where David speaks of 'the bira which I have prepared,' in reference to the future Temple.

prerequisiteKnowledge: I Chronicles 29:19 is part of David's final speech bequeathing the Temple project to Solomon.

display.title: Source for the seven-day separation: gezerah shavah from Leviticus 8
display.oneLine: Rabbi Yochanan derives both seven-day separations from Leviticus 8:34: 'to do' for the parah, 'to atone' for Yom Kippur; a gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' ties the inauguration verse to the parah statute, and the discussion continues on the next amud.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara asks where the seven-day separation comes from. Rabbi Yochanan answers from Leviticus 8:34 (the inauguration passage): 'as He commanded to do, to atone.' 'To do' is read as the parah adumah; 'to atone' is read as Yom Kippur. The whole verse cannot refer to the parah alone, since a parah does not atone. When the Gemara asks why the whole verse should not refer to Yom Kippur, it answers with a gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' (Lev 8:34 and Num 19:2): as there it is the parah, so here it is the parah, and as the inauguration had separation, so the parah requires separation. The discussion continues on the next amud.
display.whats: The Gemara asks: where does the Torah mandate the seven-day separation at all? Rabbi Yochanan answers from Leviticus 8:34 (the Tabernacle inauguration verse): 'as He commanded to do, to atone.' 'To do' refers to the parah adumah and 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. Granted, the whole verse cannot refer to the parah alone, since 'to atone' is written and a parah is not a matter of atonement; but why can't it all refer to Yom Kippur? The Gemara answers with a gezerah shavah on 'commanded/commanded' (Lev 8:34 and Num 19:2): just as the parah verse there refers to the parah, so too 'commanded' here, in the inauguration verse, refers to the parah; and just as here, at the inauguration, there is separation before the service, so too there, regarding the parah, separation is required. The discussion continues on the next amud.
display.hint: Once 'to atone' rules out reading the whole verse as the parah alone, what does the Gemara use to rule out reading the whole verse as Yom Kippur alone?

learning.learnerQuestion: How can one verse in Leviticus 8 be the source for both the Kohen Gadol's seven-day separation and the parah adumah priest's seven-day separation?
learning.coreTension: The verse seems to describe one thing (the milu'im inauguration). Making it the source for two separate laws requires first ruling out that the verse is about the heifer alone, since "to atone" doesn't fit the heifer; when a Yom-Kippur-only reading is then proposed, a word analogy is used to formally connect the heifer to the verse as well.
learning.coreMove: Elimination + gezerah shavah: first rule out reading the verse as about the heifer alone (since "to atone" doesn't fit the heifer), then, when a Yom-Kippur-only reading is proposed instead, use a shared word to formally link the verse to the heifer as well.
learning.resolution: Leviticus 8:34 is the anchor: 'to do' (parah) and 'to atone' (Yom Kippur). The gezerah shavah ('tzivah'/'tzivah' with Num 19:2) identifies 'to do' with the parah and carries the inauguration's separation over to it. The discussion continues on the next amud.

takeaway.text: A gezerah shavah can do double work: it identifies what a phrase refers to AND imports a law from the text being linked. Here it both identifies 'to do' as the heifer AND imports the sequestration rule.

reasoningPattern.notes: Two-stage derivation, and the two stages are not symmetric: the elimination argument (lines 32-34) proves only that the verse cannot be read as the parah alone; it leaves open (and explicitly raises) the possibility that the whole verse is about Yom Kippur alone. Only the gezerah shavah, via the shared verbal form 'tzivah', proves the verse must also cover the heifer.

learning.ahaMoment: The derivation is asymmetric, not symmetric: 'to atone' rules out reading the whole verse as the parah alone (a parah cannot atone), but nothing in the verse's own wording rules out reading it as Yom Kippur alone - that is exactly the objection the Gemara raises, and it can only be answered by the gezerah shavah, not by anything 'to do' itself excludes.
learning.learningBlocker: Students often read the challenge (lines 32-34) as rejecting Rabbi Yochanan's whole reading. It concedes that the verse cannot be entirely about the parah and asks only why it should not be entirely about Yom Kippur; the gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' answers that by tying 'to do' to the parah.
learning.memoryAnchor: 'Tzivah' in the parah statute (Num 19:2); 'tzivah' in the inauguration verse (Lev 8:34). The shared word licenses reading 'to do' as the parah and carrying the inauguration's separation over to it.

argumentFlow.label: Source for the seven-day rule?
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiya (via chain: Rabbi Machseya bar Idi, Rabbi Yochanan)
argumentFlow.text: From where in the Torah are both sequestration requirements derived? Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiya said that Rabbi Machseya bar Idi said that Rabbi Yochanan said they are derived from the verse about Aaron and his sons, who remained in the Tabernacle for seven days before performing the service on the eighth day of their inauguration.

argumentFlow.label: Leviticus 8:34 split
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbi Yohanan (via chain)
argumentFlow.text: 'As the Lord commanded to do, to atone': 'to do' = parah actions; 'to atone' = Yom Kippur. The milu'im verse teaches both future sequestrations.

argumentFlow.label: Why can't the whole verse apply to Yom Kippur?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Granted, the whole verse cannot be set on the parah, since 'to atone' is written and the parah is not a matter of atonement. But say the whole verse is written about Yom Kippur? Then the parah kohen's separation would have no source here.

argumentFlow.label: Gezerah shavah: tzivah/tzivah
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Derive it via verbal analogy: 'tzivah' in Lev 8:34 and 'tzivah' in Num 19:2 (the heifer statute). Just as there (Num 19) is the heifer, so here (Lev 8) refers to the heifer. And just as here (Lev 8) requires sequestration, so too there (Num 19) requires sequestration.

misconceptions.misconception: The gezerah shavah replaces Rabbi Yochanan's reading, so 'to atone' no longer teaches the Yom Kippur separation.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara's challenge concedes that 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. The gezerah shavah on 'tzivah' answers only the question about the parah, establishing that 'to do' refers to the parah and that its kohen is separated as at the inauguration.

visualizableElements.item: Verse diagram: Lev 8:34 split - 'to do' arrow to parah, 'to atone' arrow to Yom Kippur

quizSeeds.question: Which verse is the source for both seven-day sequestration rules, and how does one verse teach two laws?
quizSeeds.answer: Leviticus 8:34: 'as the Lord commanded to do, to atone.' 'To do' refers to the parah adumah; 'to atone' refers to Yom Kippur. Only the parah-alone reading is textually excluded (a parah cannot atone); the Gemara itself raises the possibility that the whole verse describes Yom Kippur alone, and that is ruled out only by the gezerah shavah that follows, not by 'to do' on its own.

quizSeeds.question: Why can't Leviticus 8:34 refer only to Yom Kippur?
quizSeeds.answer: The gezerah shavah answers this: the shared word 'tzivah' in the heifer statute (Numbers 19:2) and in Leviticus 8:34 shows that 'to do' in Leviticus 8:34 must refer to the heifer - so the verse cannot be entirely about Yom Kippur, since part of it ('to do') belongs to the parah.

quizSeeds.question: What two verses are linked by the gezerah shavah, and what word is shared?
quizSeeds.answer: Leviticus 8:34 ('the Lord commanded to do') and Numbers 19:2 ('the statute that the Lord commanded'). The shared word is 'tzivah' (commanded).

prerequisiteKnowledge: Leviticus 8:34 is from the milu'im inauguration narrative.
Numbers 19:2 is the introduction to the parah adumah statute.

glossary.en: The private chamber in the Temple where the Kohen Gadol lived during the seven days before Yom Kippur, separated from his home in case a disqualification should prevent him from serving.
Red Heifer. A cow burned by a priest who is sequestered seven days beforehand; the ritual is performed using dung, stone, and earth vessels, which cannot become ritually impure.

A person who immersed in a mikveh today but hasn't yet reached sunset. The Sages deliberately assigned such a person (tvul yom) to burn the Red Heifer, in order to publicly reject the Sadducees' stated position that the ritual required waiting until sunset.
Verbal analogy. When the same word or phrase appears in two Torah passages, the rules of one passage carry over to the other. One of the thirteen principles of biblical interpretation.

The seven-day inauguration ceremony for the Mishkan priesthood. Aaron and his sons remained in the Tabernacle seven days before beginning service on the eighth day. This is the template from which the seven-day separation rule is derived.

rashiTranslations.en: "Seven days before Yom Kippur they separate the Kohen Gadol" - because the entire Yom Kippur service
is valid only when performed by the appointed High Priest, as derived in Horayot (last chapter, 12b).
Scripture says regarding Yom Kippur: "the kohen who is anointed shall make atonement" - limiting the service to the Kohen Gadol.
The Gemara (6a) explains why the separation is necessary. "To the Parhedrin chamber" - that was the chamber's name.
The Gemara explains why the chamber bore that name.
"And they prepare for him" - they designate another kohen to serve as High Priest in his place,
should some disqualifying event befall the Kohen Gadol before Yom Kippur.
The possible disqualification: a seminal emission (keri) or other impurity that bars entry to the Temple.
"And for his household" - this phrase about the Yom Kippur atonement appears in Acharei Mot.
"If so" - Rabbi Yehudah requires preparing a backup wife lest the first die before Yom Kippur.
Since he feared death - "there is no end to the matter"
Perhaps the second wife too will die - the objection stands. The Gemara now opens. "The burning of the cow" -
"of the cow" refers to the Parah Adumah (red heifer). "On the face of the Birah" - the chamber's location.
"The Birah" - the Gemara below explains what this term means.
"To the north-east" - the chamber was in the northeastern corner of the Temple courtyard.
"All its rites" of the Parah Adumah had to be performed with implements not susceptible to impurity.
"Vessels of dung" (klei gelalin) - implements made from dried cattle dung, which cannot receive impurity.
These three vessel types are explained in Menachot, in the chapter of Rabbi Yishmael.
"Vessels of earth" (klei adamah) - not kiln-fired earthenware,
but rather made from the earth itself, not fired like earthenware in a kiln.
That is, [earth] that is like soft stone, from which vessels are hollowed out.
"What is the reason" the Sages required these non-susceptible vessels for the Parah Adumah?
"Because a tevul yom is valid for the Parah Adumah" - the Gemara derives this below,
in the chapter "Taraf BaKalpi" (Yoma 43b), from the verse "and the pure one shall sprinkle."
"So that they not treat it lightly" -
people might reason: since even a tevul yom is kosher for the Parah Adumah,
perhaps there is no need to be scrupulous about its purity requirements.
Therefore the Sages imposed many rabbinic stringencies of purity upon the Parah Adumah,
and this is one of those stringencies. "Since it is a sin-offering [chatat]" -
the Parah Adumah is called a chatat, as Scripture says in Numbers 19:
"It is for purification waters, it is a sin-offering." "And a sin-offering requires the north" -
regular sin-offerings brought on the altar are slaughtered in the northern part of the courtyard.
This does not mean the Parah Adumah itself must be slaughtered in the north -
it was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives, outside the Temple entirely.
"And it is written" regarding the cow (Numbers 19): "opposite the face of the Tent of Meeting" -
during the blood-sprinkling ceremony, the kohen stands on the Mount of Olives
and aims toward the entrance of the Sanctuary, which is in the eastern wall of the Temple.
"So that there be a distinguishing mark" - the northeastern chamber signals to all
that this kohen was separated there specifically for the Parah Adumah service.
The visible separation imposes the Parah Adumah service upon him formally,
since that service is called a chatat and requires an eastern orientation; the kohen must
focus his heart on performing all its rites carefully and in the correct sequence.
"The Bira which I prepared" - David's statement in Chronicles about the Temple site.
David designated the threshing-floor of Aravna the Jebusite as the site for the Temple,
and it is King David speaking this verse in Chronicles.
"From where are these matters derived?" - what is the scriptural source for the seven-day separation?
that separation is required for both Yom Kippur and the red heifer. "As he did" - just as Moses separated Aaron and his sons for seven days before the inaugural service of the Mishkan.
At the inauguration (milu'im), God commanded them to remain separated from their homes for seven days.
As Leviticus 8 states: they were to remain at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting
"day and night" - the full seven days of the inauguration period.
On the eighth day they performed the actual inaugural service, as Leviticus 9 records.
"On the eighth day [Moses] called" (Leviticus 9) and then: "approach the altar" - service followed seven days of preparation.
"As he commanded" - this pattern of seven-day separation before a major service applies to all future generations.
"To do" - to perform. The separation of seven days is required before the one-day service of Yom Kippur
"Before the performance" means: the preparatory period precedes the fulfillment of the mitzvah.
"But say [rather]" - the Gemara introduces an objection to this derivation.
